params.linkText: Nasdaq’s Business Is Outrunning Its Stock

children: Nasdaq

is beginning to charge customers for artificial intelligence agents used in financial crime management, as the company pursues growth across its technology, data and index businesses, Chief Financial Officer Sarah Youngwood said at an RBC Capital Markets technology conference.

Of Nasdaq’s 2,800 financial crime management clients, 850 are using its agentic workforce and 70 are paying for it, Youngwood said. The agents can perform full tasks and deliver fourfold efficiencies for clients, she said. Nasdaq expects to introduce similar capabilities across products including Calypso, AxiomSL and surveillance.

children: Youngwood said adoption and bank AI governance reviews are important steps before customers begin paying. The 850 users have gone through a rigorous process at banks, she said, adding that the initial conversion to paid customers was encouraging.
Financial Crime and Capital Markets Technology

Nasdaq’s Verafin financial crime business has gained traction with larger banks after initially serving small and midsize institutions. RBC Capital Markets analyst Ashish Sabadra said the company signed 12 enterprise customers through the third quarter, compared with nine in all of 2025; Youngwood confirmed the figures.

children: Youngwood attributed the momentum in part to Nasdaq’s brand and its existing relationships with large financial institutions. She also pointed to the value of consortium data drawn from 2,800 banks, which she said can help identify activity spanning multiple institutions.

Nasdaq estimates its serviceable addressable market at $38 billion, including $8 billion in financial crime management, Youngwood said. Half of the financial crime opportunity is with large banks, where the company started with limited penetration. Most of the 850 customers currently using its AI agents are smaller banks, but Nasdaq has begun discussing the capabilities with larger institutions, she said.

Capital Markets Technology posted 19% annual recurring revenue growth, Youngwood said, citing demand for trade management services, connectivity and modernization of market infrastructure. She cautioned that third-quarter growth also benefited from some outsized items, including pricing catch-up and additional testing. The extra testing is expected to continue in the fourth quarter and taper off at the beginning of next year.
Regulatory Technology and Index Growth

RegTech delivered 15% annual recurring revenue growth, according to Sabadra. Youngwood said Nasdaq’s AxiomSL regulatory reporting product serves all but one non-Chinese global systemically important bank. Nasdaq has also developed a simpler version for smaller banks, creating opportunities to sell it to Calypso and Verafin customers, she said.

Youngwood said AxiomSL now covers 174 regulators and 66 countries, compared with 110 regulators and 55 countries when Nasdaq acquired it. She added that demand for surveillance is expanding as markets move toward longer trading hours and new participants, including prediction market and digital asset firms, seek the service.

Nasdaq’s index business grew 39% in the latest quarter, Youngwood said, benefiting from the broader shift toward passive investing and demand for products tied to the Nasdaq-100. She also cited opportunities in index options, futures, institutional products and thematic indexes.

On listings, Youngwood described a strong pipeline spanning the AI supply chain, health care and defense, while noting that the timing of listings depends on several factors. She also cited recent listing switches by Walmart, Hilton and GM.
Digital Assets and Capital Allocation
Nasdaq is targeting a move to trading 23 hours a day, five days a week, by Dec. 6, Youngwood said. Longer trading hours are also supporting demand for market data from brokerage firms, she added.

The company is working with Kraken on a Nasdaq equity token that would let issuers choose to offer a token of their stock while keeping it connected to the existing liquidity pool. Youngwood said the offering is expected in the first half of next year.

Nasdaq is launching binary options but does not plan to participate in sports or political prediction markets, Youngwood said. The company has not entered perpetuals and wants to understand institutional demand and see appropriate regulated frameworks, she added.

On capital allocation, Youngwood said Nasdaq will focus on organic growth while continuing to consider smaller acquisitions. The company generated $2.3 billion in free cash flow over the prior 12 months and repurchased $1.2 billion of shares in the prior nine months, compared with $600 million in the year-earlier period, she said. Nasdaq is already within its target leverage range, she added.
About Nasdaq

Nasdaq, Inc. is a global technology and financial markets company best known for operating the Nasdaq Stock Market. Its exchange services support the listing and trading of equities and other financial products, and the company provides market data and trading technology to exchanges, brokers, investors, and other financial institutions. Nasdaq also develops software and services for financial institutions and corporations, including solutions for regulatory compliance, market surveillance, and the detection and prevention of financial crime.
